paragraph_text.text: The lowest share in the country, outside college counties

Our Rentals Within Reach tool measures how many of a county's rentals its median renter household could afford, spending 30% of its income after taxes on rent. In 2020-2024, Gwinnett County, Georgia, had the lowest share of the 1,922 counties we ranked, leaving out college counties.

image.alt: Bar chart of the 10 counties with the lowest share of rentals within reach in 2020-2024, leaving out college counties. Gwinnett County, Georgia, is lowest at 10.5%, followed by Clayton County, Georgia, at 11.0%, Lincoln County, New Mexico, at 11.8% and DeKalb County, Georgia, at 14.0%. The rest range from 14.2% to 15.4%.

source_text.text: Source: Data 4 The People, Rentals Within Reach, from Census Bureau American Community Survey 5-year estimates, 2020-2024.

paragraph_text.text: Two caveats. Clayton County, also in metro Atlanta, is only half a point behind. And with college counties included, Gwinnett ranks third, behind Whitman County, Washington, and Benton County, Oregon. Three of the four lowest counties on this list are in the Atlanta area.
A 59% decline

In 2005-2009, 25.5% of Gwinnett's rentals were within reach of its median renter household. By 2020-2024, 10.5% were. The national share was 32% at the start and 31% at the end. Gwinnett added rentals over those years, but the number within reach still fell.

image.alt: Stacked bar chart of Gwinnett County rentals in four periods. All rentals grew from 65,800 in 2005-2009 to 85,500, 97,300 and 107,200 in 2020-2024. Rentals within reach were 16,800 (25.5%), then 15,500 (18.1%), then 20,900 (21.5%), then 11,300 (10.5%).

source_text.text: Source: Data 4 The People, Rentals Within Reach, from Census Bureau American Community Survey 5-year estimates. Rentals within reach are the tool's share times its count of rentals.

paragraph_text.text: Rent rose 32%. Renter income rose 8%.

After inflation, Gwinnett's median rent rose 32% from 2005-2009 to 2020-2024, while its median renter household income rose 8%. Among the 15 Atlanta-area counties with at least 10,000 renter households, Gwinnett's gap between the two was one of the widest.

image.alt: Scatter plot of 15 Atlanta-area counties, with the change in median renter income across and the change in median rent up, 2005-2009 to 2020-2024, after inflation. Gwinnett, at income up 8% and rent up 32%, sits farthest above the line where the two rose at the same rate. Clayton, DeKalb and Cherokee are close behind it.

source_text.text: Source: Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year estimates; BLS consumer price index. Gwinnett's income change has a margin of about 5 points either way.

paragraph_text.text: Home prices rose fast in Gwinnett, but they rose about as fast in Cobb County, where renters' income rose 18%.
New rentals came in out of reach

Gwinnett added about 41,000 rentals over this period. Two kinds account for more than half of them: about 11,300 older houses, built before 2000, that became rentals, and about 11,000 apartments built since 2010. Neither was priced for the median renter household, which could afford about $1,250 a month at 30% of its income. In 2020-2024, older houses rented for a median of about $1,990 and new apartments for $1,870. About 10% of the older houses and 8% of the new apartments were within reach. Houses built since 2010 rented for more still.

image.alt: Bar chart of median monthly rent in Gwinnett County in 2020-2024, against the $1,250 the median renter household could afford. Houses built before 2000 $1,990, with 10% within reach. Apartments built 2010 or later $1,870, with 8% within reach. Houses built 2010 or later $2,500, with 2% within reach.

source_text.text: Source: Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year microdata. Rents include utilities.

paragraph_text.text: That does not explain why the number of rentals within reach fell. The answer is in older apartments, built before 2000. Gwinnett had about the same number of them in both periods, but their median rent went from about $860 to $1,660, up 92%. After inflation, that is a 31% rise, while the amount the median renter household could afford rose 8%. In 2005-2009, the median older apartment rented for about $100 more than that amount. By 2020-2024, it was about $400 more.

image.alt: Bar chart of Gwinnett County amounts in 2024 dollars. In 2005-2009, the median rent for apartments built before 2000 was $1,260, and the median renter household could afford $1,160. In 2020-2024, the median rent was $1,660, and the household could afford $1,250.

source_text.text: Source: Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year microdata; Data 4 The People, Rentals Within Reach. Amounts in 2024 dollars.

paragraph_text.text: In other words, the rentals new to the market came in out of reach, and the older apartments that used to be close to reach rose far faster than renters' income.
Renters' pay did not keep up

Why did renter income not keep up? For the same kind of renter household (the same number of workers, and a householder of the same age and education), income fell about 3% after inflation. Renter households as a whole earned more only because the households changed: more members worked, more worked full time, and more householders were older or had college degrees. Pay itself did not rise. After inflation, the median renter who worked full time all year earned about $46,100 in 2005-2009 and $44,600 in 2020-2024. In Cobb, that pay rose 7%.

image.alt: Bar chart of the change in median earnings of renters who worked full time all year, 2005-2009 to 2020-2024, after inflation. Fulton up 21.2%, DeKalb up 9.9%, Cobb up 6.7%, Gwinnett down 3.3%, Henry down 3.4%, Cherokee down 6.0% and Clayton down 9.2%.

source_text.text: Source: Census Bureau, American Community Survey 5-year microdata; BLS consumer price index. Gwinnett's change has a margin of about 5 points either way.

paragraph_text.text: Renter pay also fell in Henry, Cherokee and Clayton. In Gwinnett, rents rose about as much as in Cobb, while pay moved more like Henry's.
[Eric: closing]
What this does not tell you
Why. These are patterns that came alongside the rise in rents. The data does not show what caused them.

Survey estimates. Every number comes from a survey and has a margin of error. Gwinnett's lead over Clayton, and over the next counties in the Atlanta comparison, is small enough that the order could change.
One way to measure affordability. "Within reach" uses the tool's default: the median renter household, after taxes, paying 30% of income. Other settings give other rankings.
Different people. The survey takes two snapshots of different renters. It does not follow the same people over time.
Year built. Households report when their building was built, and some may not know exactly.
How we did this

Shares within reach come from our Rentals Within Reach tool, built from Census Bureau American Community Survey 5-year estimates for 2005-2009, 2010-2014, 2015-2019 and 2020-2024. Counties with fewer than 1,000 rentals, or with unreliable estimates, are left out. College counties are the tool's 71 counties where 15% or more of residents age 3 and over are enrolled in college.
Rent and income changes use the published median gross rent and median renter household income, put in 2024 dollars with the consumer price index.

Rentals by building type and year built, rents of older apartments, and renter pay, come from the survey's microdata (individual household records) for Gwinnett and six neighboring counties. Forsyth County is left out of these because its 2005-2009 records also cover Dawson and Pickens counties. Full time means 35 or more hours a week for 50 or more weeks a year.
Home prices come from the Federal Housing Finance Agency's county house price index.
An independent check recomputed every number from the raw data. The code and data notes are on GitHub.
